claim: In the discussion of tax-exempt, Chapter 19 excludes a contrasting syntactic construction in which a noun or NP modifies an adjective.
evidence_summary: Chapter 6 identifies the NPs in two inches long, a foot wide and a bit lax as modifiers of adjectives. Chapter 19 later acknowledges the measure phrase and contrasts it with compound forms.
finding: The general wording in §4.1 conflicts with CGEL’s own phrasal cases. Tax-exempt can retain its compound analysis.
proposed_wording: Tax-exempt is a compound adjective. A limited range of NPs can also modify adjectives in phrases such as two inches long and a bit lax.
inference: Does English have a syntactic construction in which an adjective takes an NP modifier?

evidence.source: Geoffrey K. Pullum and Rodney Huddleston (2002). CGEL, Chapter 6, Adjectives and adverbs.
evidence.passage: Ch. 19 §4.1, p. 1644. In its discussion of tax-exempt, CGEL excludes a contrasting syntactic construction with a noun or NP modifying an adjective.
evidence.example: Chapter 6 explicitly assigns NP modifier function to two inches in two inches long and lists a foot wide and a bit lax alongside it.
evidence.establishes: CGEL’s adjective-phrase analysis provides cases outside the blanket statement in Chapter 19.

evidence.source: Laurie Bauer and Rodney Huddleston (2002). CGEL, Chapter 19, Lexical word-formation.
evidence.passage: Ch. 19 §4.1, p. 1644. In its discussion of tax-exempt, CGEL excludes a contrasting syntactic construction with a noun or NP modifying an adjective.
evidence.example: Section 4.3.1 acknowledges a restricted set of NP dependents. Section 4.3.3 uses three inches long as the phrasal comparison for singular-unit compounds.
evidence.establishes: Chapter 19 itself supplies the qualification. The local compound analysis of tax-exempt remains available.
